Remember where cartilage is found in the airways. Which tubes have C-shaped cartilage or plates, and which tubes have lost cartilage completely?
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 - what type of epithelium is this?**

Look at the right image. You can see lots of tall cells with cilia on top, plus paler goblet cells squeezed between them. These are tall columnar cells, not flat squamous cells.

This is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, typical of the trachea and bronchi. So statement 1 is false because it says squamous.

**Check statement 2 - can you see smooth muscle?**

Now look at the low power image on the left. From top to bottom you have: folded epithelium, then a thin connective tissue layer with blood vessels, then a thin darker band of smooth muscle, then a very thick pale layer below.

That thin band is smooth muscle, which contracts to constrict the airway. So statement 2 is true.

**Check statement 3 - does cartilage rule out a bronchiole?**

The very thick pale layer at the bottom with small scattered nuclei is hyaline cartilage. It keeps larger airways open.

Remember the rule: trachea and bronchi have cartilage, bronchioles have smooth muscle but no cartilage. So if cartilage is visible, it cannot be a bronchiole. Statement 3 is true.

True statements are 2 and 3 only, which is option D.

options.A: Incorrect, as it includes statement 1. The epithelium is ciliated columnar, not squamous, so 1 is false.
options.B: Incorrect, as it includes statement 1 and misses statement 3. Statement 1 is false and statement 3 is true.
options.C: Incorrect, as it includes statement 1. Goblet cells are present but they sit between ciliated columnar cells, not squamous cells.
options.D: Correct. Statement 2 is true as smooth muscle is visible, and statement 3 is true as cartilage proves it is not a bronchiole.
